title: The Price of a Thousand Slaps (TE)
summary: A palace guard demands half the reward of a fisherman presenting an enormous fish to Akbar. Birbal ensures the guard receives his exact half of 'one thousand slaps.' [TE]
full_text:
A poor fisherman named Mangal caught an extraordinary, silver-scaled Mahseer fish in the Yamuna river—a creature of magnificent size and beauty, worthy of an emperor's banquet. He carried the fish in a wet basket to the palace gates of Agra to present it as a gift to Emperor Akbar.

At the outer gate, a corrupt and arrogant sentry named Dilawar blocked his path:

'You cannot enter, peasant! Unless you sign a pledge promising to give me exactly half of whatever reward the Emperor bestows upon you today, I will throw you and your fish into the moat!'

The fisherman agreed and entered the Diwan-i-Khas.

Akbar was delighted with the magnificent fish: 'Fisherman, this is the finest fish ever brought to my kitchens! Ask for whatever reward you desire, and it shall be granted!'

Mangal bowed low: 'Your Majesty, grant me one thousand hard slaps across my face by your royal guards!'

Akbar was horrified: 'Are you out of your mind? I wish to give you gold, and you ask for one thousand slaps?'

The fisherman insisted: 'It is my only request, Sire.'

Akbar reluctantly ordered a guard to administer the slaps gently. After fifty gentle slaps had been struck, the fisherman held up his hand:

'Halt, Your Majesty! I have a partner at the palace gate. Sentry Dilawar made me sign a contract swearing to surrender exactly half of my reward before letting me enter! I have taken fifty; he is entitled to the remaining nine hundred and fifty slaps!'

Akbar's face turned crimson with imperial rage. He had Dilawar dragged into the court in chains.

Akbar commanded the chief executioner: 'Administer nine hundred and fifty fierce slaps to this corrupt scoundrel, and banish him from imperial service!'

After the crooked sentry was beaten and hauled away, Akbar presented the clever fisherman with one thousand gold mohurs, and Birbal remarked that greed always signs its own punishment.
